Ask another member of the clinical team (not yourself) to approach the patient to explain the incident and seek his informed consent for blood-borne virus (HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C) testing.
explanation:
Following a sharps injury:
1. Perform immediate first aid: gently encourage bleeding under running water, wash with soap and water (never scrub or suck the wound), and cover with a waterproof dressing.
2. Contact Occupational Health (or ED out of hours) immediately—HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is most effective when started within 1 hour and must be started within 72 hours.
3. Source-patient testing for HIV, HBV, and HCV requires explicit informed consent in a capacitous patient (under the Human Tissue Act 2004, testing blood without consent is unlawful), and UK guidance specifically states that **another clinician** (not the injured healthcare worker) should obtain that consent to avoid placing undue emotional pressure on the patient.

scenario:
You are a GP trainee. Halfway through a consultation with a 58-year-old man discussing newly diagnosed heart failure, you notice that his smartphone on the desk has its voice-recorder app actively running and recording your conversation. He did not ask you beforehand.

Select the THREE most appropriate actions to take in this situation.
options: Refuse to speak for the remainder of the appointment and communicate only by typing on your screen.
Call practice security to confiscate his smartphone under the Data Protection Act.
Terminate the consultation immediately and remove him from the practice list for a breach of trust.
Threaten him with legal action for recording you without written permission.
Reassure him that he is welcome to record the consultation openly for his personal use to help remember the plan, and offer to also provide a written summary or patient information leaflet.
Acknowledge the recording calmly and non-defensively, and ask him what prompted him to record the consultation (for example, anxiety about forgetting complex medical information).
Demand that he hand over his phone and delete the audio file in front of you before you will prescribe his heart failure medication.
Continue the consultation professionally and document in the clinical records that the consultation was audio-recorded by the patient.
correct_answer: Acknowledge the recording calmly and non-defensively, and ask him what prompted him to record the consultation (for example, anxiety about forgetting complex medical information).
Reassure him that he is welcome to record the consultation openly for his personal use to help remember the plan, and offer to also provide a written summary or patient information leaflet.
Continue the consultation professionally and document in the clinical records that the consultation was audio-recorded by the patient.
explanation:
Medical defence organisations (MDU/MPS) and the BMA highlight that the clinical information discussed in a consultation belongs to the patient (it is *their* personal data), so a patient recording a consultation for their own personal use does not breach data protection law. Most patients record consultations because they are anxious, hard of hearing, or worried about forgetting complex advice, or want to share the explanation with a relative. The most professional approach is to:
1. Address it calmly and explore why they felt the need to record covertly.
2. Reassure them that open recording is fine and offer written summaries/leaflets to support understanding.
3. Deliver the same high standard of care and note in the medical record that the consultation was recorded.

scenario:
You are an FY2 doctor working in the Emergency Department. A uniformed police officer approaches the reception desk and asks you for the names, addresses, and clinical notes of all patients who have attended the department over the last 48 hours with a dog bite, because a local resident reported being bitten by an off-lead dog in the park yesterday and the police are trying to trace other potential victims or the owner. The officer does not have a court order or patient consent.

Select the THREE most appropriate actions to take in this situation.
options: Consult the Emergency Department consultant on call or the hospital Caldicott Guardian/information governance team and document the police request.
Tell the officer that doctors are never allowed to speak to the police even if there is a court order.
Call the patients yourself and tell them the police will arrest them if they do not go to the police station.
Print out the full Emergency Department attendance list for the last 48 hours and hand it to the officer immediately.
Politely decline to release the names, addresses, or clinical records of patients without their consent or a court order/statutory requirement.
Access the electronic health records of all dog-bite patients from the last week and leave the computer screen unlocked while you go for a coffee so the officer can read it.

Explain to the police officer that confidentiality can only be breached without consent in the public interest if there is a risk of death or very serious harm (such as gun or knife wounds or terrorism), and ask if they can provide further details or obtain a court order.
Give the officer the names and phone numbers verbally so there is no paper trail of the disclosure.
correct_answer: Politely decline to release the names, addresses, or clinical records of patients without their consent or a court order/statutory requirement.

Explain to the police officer that confidentiality can only be breached without consent in the public interest if there is a risk of death or very serious harm (such as gun or knife wounds or terrorism), and ask if they can provide further details or obtain a court order.
Consult the Emergency Department consultant on call or the hospital Caldicott Guardian/information governance team and document the police request.
explanation:
Under GMC *Confidentiality* guidance, the police have no automatic right to access patient health records without the patient's explicit consent unless disclosure is required by statute, ordered by a judge/court, or justified in the public interest to prevent or detect a *very serious crime* (such as murder, manslaughter, rape, child abuse, or gun/knife attacks—where the GMC has specific gunshot and knife wound reporting guidance). A general fishing enquiry for dog-bite attendees without consent or a court order does not meet that threshold. You should:
1. Politely decline immediate disclosure.
2. Explain the threshold for disclosure without consent (consent, court order, or serious risk of death/serious harm).
3. Seek advice from your senior consultant or Caldicott Guardian and document the interaction.

scenario:
You are an FY1 doctor. While scrolling through Instagram during your lunch break, you see a public story posted 20 minutes ago by a final-year medical student attached to your firm. The photo shows the student smiling in scrubs at the nurses' station with the caption 'Surviving another long ward round!'. In the background behind his shoulder, the ward patient whiteboard is clearly visible and legible, showing several patients' full names, bed numbers, and diagnoses.

Select the THREE most appropriate actions to take in this situation.
options: Tell the ward sister that you took the photo yourself so the medical student does not get into trouble with the university.
Ignore the post because the student did not intend to show the whiteboard and stories disappear after 24 hours anyway.
Contact the medical student immediately in private, explain that patient names and diagnoses are visible on the whiteboard in the background, and ask him to delete the post straight away.
Screenshot the post and share it in the hospital junior doctors' WhatsApp group to warn everyone about the student.
Discuss GMC guidance on social media and patient confidentiality with the student so he understands why taking photographs in clinical areas is unsafe.
Delete the patients' names from the physical ward whiteboard so they no longer match the photograph.
Inform your supervising consultant or clinical supervisor and report the inadvertent data breach via the hospital incident reporting system (Datix) in line with information governance policy.
Leave a public comment underneath the Instagram post listing which patients' names are visible so his followers know it was an accident.
correct_answer: Contact the medical student immediately in private, explain that patient names and diagnoses are visible on the whiteboard in the background, and ask him to delete the post straight away.
Inform your supervising consultant or clinical supervisor and report the inadvertent data breach via the hospital incident reporting system (Datix) in line with information governance policy.
Discuss GMC guidance on social media and patient confidentiality with the student so he understands why taking photographs in clinical areas is unsafe.
explanation:
Accidental visibility of patient-identifiable data (whiteboards, computer screens, notes) in clinical selfies is a common and serious confidentiality and UK GDPR breach covered by GMC social media guidance.
1. The immediate priority is damage limitation: contact the student privately right away so the public post is removed immediately.
2. Because patient-identifiable data was published online, you must escalate to the clinical supervisor and log an information governance incident (Datix) as required by trust policy.
3. Providing constructive educational feedback on GMC social media rules helps prevent future breaches. Sharing screenshots on WhatsApp only propagates the data breach further, and taking false blame is dishonest.

scenario:
You are a surgical FY2 doctor in the pre-operative assessment clinic reviewing a 62-year-old woman scheduled for an elective total hip replacement in 2 weeks. She is a practising Jehovah's Witness with full mental capacity and presents a valid, signed, and witnessed Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT) stating that she refuses transfusion of whole blood, red cells, white cells, platelets, and plasma under all circumstances, even if her life is at risk. Her preoperative haemoglobin is 108 g/L with a low mean cell volume (MCV 74 fL) and low serum ferritin.

Select the THREE most appropriate actions to take in this situation.
options: Wait until she is unconscious in theatre and then ask her non-Jehovah's Witness husband to consent to a blood transfusion on her behalf.
Prescribe a preoperative red blood cell transfusion disguised in an opaque bag and tell her it is intravenous saline.
Cancel her hip replacement permanently and discharge her without discussing the case with the surgical or anaesthetic consultants.
Inform the consultant orthopaedic surgeon and consultant anaesthetist early so that a multidisciplinary bloodless-surgery perioperative plan can be agreed in advance.
Tell her that if she suffers life-threatening haemorrhage while under general anaesthesia, the anaesthetist will override her wishes and transfuse red cells to save her life.
Optimise her preoperative haemoglobin before surgery by investigating and treating her iron-deficiency anaemia (e.g. with oral or intravenous iron therapy).

Accept the luxury spa weekend, attend the 30-minute talk, and switch 50 patients to the new drug on Monday morning.

Decline the offer of the luxury hotel weekend and refuse to enter into any agreement linking personal hospitality to prescribing changes.

Inform your fellow GP partners (and practice governance lead) about the representative's inappropriate inducement.
